items.title: Woman’s Bold Biblical Mission to ‘Capture … Souls From Hell’
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "I want to see people come to Jesus."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Ministry leader Bunni Pounds is on a mission to encourage Americans to crack open their Bibles and learn more about the Lord.

Pounds, founder of the newly minted Bunni Pounds Ministries, told CBN News her previous mission of motivating Christians to vote has been replaced by efforts to spark interest in the Bible. Her America Reads the Bible initiative earlier this year ignited Bible interest among millions of people, with three million watching as 500 national leaders read through the entire Bible.

“I’ve spent the last seven years of my life trying to mobilize Christians to pray, vote, engage through Christians Engaged,” she said. “But America Reads the Bible shifted my entire life and our team, and we just realized there’s a root problem more below the surface than just Christians engaging and voting.”

Pounds believes America has a biblical literacy problem. And seeing how America Reads the Bible took form motivated her to seek more of a biblical impact.

“It impacted so many people in this country,” she said of the effort. “And I realized we’ve got to pour gasoline on this. We’ve got to really reach the younger generation, and so we launched the ministry with the idea that we are going to lead thousands of people through a Bible study created with Great American Pure Flix with this content.”

Pounds and her ministry are inviting people to go through the Bible together over a 24-week period starting Jan. 1; she’s calling the effort The Whole Bible Live. Pounds is also planning yet another national event in 2028, along with other local efforts.

“At the end of the day, I want to see people come to Jesus,” Pounds said, explaining what success for her new ministry might look like. “I want to see people be discipled, and I want to see people become disciple makers, and so success looks like hundreds of thousands of people, in the next five years, going through the Bible, becoming the leaders that God’s called them to be, understanding who they truly are in Christ, and taking on the culture, and bringing truth into culture.”

Pounds said young people are hungry and “desperate for God” — and she delivered an important reminder for believers.

“We’re not fighting against people that we disagree with,” she said. “God is after people’s hearts. He’s trying to capture their souls from hell.”

Pounds said she believes America is at a turning point and that Christians need to be encouraging everyone to turn to the Lord. She encouraged people to go to Bunni Pounds Ministries and take part in the Whole Bible Live.

“We need Jesus in this moment,” Pounds said.

items.title: Are Demons Real? New Data Reveals Americans’ Experience With Spiritual Attacks
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: Wow.
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Spiritual warfare is a real part of the human experience, and the Bible explicitly details how events in the spiritual realm affect people.

“For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this dark world and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms,” Ephesians 6:12 (NIV) reads, with verse 13 continuing: “Therefore put on the full armor of God, so that when the day of evil comes, you may be able to stand your ground, and after you have done everything, to stand.”

The question isn’t if people will experience spiritual warfare; it’s when. A new survey from the American Bible Society (ABS) explores what Americans believe about spiritual warfare, specifically measuring how many people believe they have faced such attacks (watch CBN’s documentary “Investigating the Supernatural: Angels and Demons” today).

Dr. John Plake, editor-in-chief of the State of the Bible series and chief innovation officer at ABS, told CBN News that around 1-in-4 Americans report facing spiritual warfare.

“We saw real difference here across levels of faith participation,” he said. “About a fourth — 26% — of American adults say they’ve had that experience.”

He continued, “[Fifty-eight percent] of practicing Christians would agree with that statement, casual Christians, 28%, nominal Christians, 24%, and then non-Christians, 10%.”

The topic itself is quite fascinating, as Plake said it’s sometimes hard to quantify what a spiritual attack denotes. And since there’s not “a lot of deep data” there’s not qualitative information to help understand what respondents believe a spiritual attack looked like or entailed.

“I’m sure these people do have stories that they can tell about times when they felt like the negative experiences that they were having couldn’t be attributed just to natural causes, that there was some form of spiritual opposition that was going on,” Plake said. “And to see that incidence be that high, I was pretty fascinated by it.”

Another factor ABS was able to screen for was people’s reaction to a perceived spiritual attack — and those statistics were equally interesting.

“So 74% of people who [said they faced attack] said that the way they respond to spiritual attack is that they pray,” Plake said. “I think that makes a lot of sense, right? When spiritual attacks come, you may not be in a particular context where it’s easy to do much else, but you can always pray.”

The second-highest percentage was 36%, who said they declare Christ’s authority.

“There is this kind of sense that … they’re aware they’re in a spiritual battle, that their opposition isn’t … the person who may be opposing them at the moment,” Plake said. “But actually, there’s a spiritual thing going on here, and so they declare Christ’s authority.”

Next came the 24% who said they listen to praise and worship music, but then there’s the smallest — and most concerning — percentage: the 15% who said that they meditate on or quote Scripture.

“I would have hoped that would be a little bit higher,” Plake said. “And I think it also presents an opportunity for pastors and church leaders to recognize, ‘Hey, there are a lot of people, particularly in the church, who are having these experiences, and how can we equip them biblically to respond when they’re facing these kinds of spiritual attacks or moments of opposition, or even when there’s a need for a miraculous healing?'”

For more on this topic, watch “Investigating the Supernatural: Angels and Demons.”

To him, the colonies are British, and the Crown is the source and protector of the very
items.content:
📖 News | Christian Headlines
Benjamin Clem is a teenager in 1770s colonial America who believes in the patriots’ fight for freedom and isn’t afraid to say so to anyone who sides with the British.His brother Jeremiah sees things differently. To him, the colonies are British, and the Crown is the source and protector of the very rights the patriots claim to be fighting for.The brothers might find it easier to live with their differences if they lived apart. Instead, they share a roof with their widowed mother. Their father died on the voyage across the Atlantic when a French vessel attacked the British ship carrying the family.Benjamin and Jeremiah both watched their father die, but they disagree on what he gave his life for.“You betray all he fought for,” Jeremiah tells Benjamin one night at the dinner table as their mother tries to keep the peace.“Father didn't die for England – he died for us,” Benjamin retorts. “He said this was the only place we could truly be free.” “The new world is the same as the old one,” Jeremiah responds. “Father didn't live to see it, but I have.”Soon, the brothers find themselves on opposite sides of the battlefield in the Revolutionary War, each convinced he’s fighting for a just cause and growing more resentful of the other for choosing the opposite side.It’s all part of the new Angel Studios movie Drummer Boy (PG-13), which stars Joel Smallbone of For King & Country as Jeremiah, Lucas Leach as Benjamin,p and Charles Esten (Nashville) as a British officer, Lord Balfour. Smallbone and his brother Luke wrote the music. Another Smallbone, Ben, co-directed it alongside Joel. Here are three reasons families will probably love it:Photo Credit: ©Angel Studios

items.title: Joel Smallbone and the Brother He Drifted From Just Made a Movie About Brothers at War
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: At one point, Joel Smallbone and his brother Ben went their separate ways. “You could argue we ended up on our own sort of opposite sides of life’s battlefield,” Smallbone says. What brought them back together was a movie about the same thing. “I remember saying, wouldn’t it be fascinating if two br
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

At one point, Joel Smallbone and his brother Ben went their separate ways. “You could argue we ended up on our own sort of opposite sides of life’s battlefield,” Smallbone says. What brought them back together was a movie about the same thing.

“I remember saying, wouldn’t it be fascinating if two brothers who’ve had ideological differences and creative differences came back together behind the camera to tell a story about two brothers that end up on opposite sides of a literal war?”

That movie is Drummer Boy, a Revolutionary War Christmas musical that opened in theaters Nov. 6. Joel and Ben co-directed it, and Joel plays Jeremiah Clem. The cast includes Ioan Gruffudd and Melora Hardin (Jan from The Office).

It took a while. Smallbone, who sings in for KING + COUNTRY with his brother Luke, pitched it to Lionsgate on March 10, 2020, and, by his account, the studio nearly greenlit it.

“And then March the 13th happened and the world shut down,” he says. Unsung Hero came first and the musical waited. Someone eventually reminded him 2026 is America’s 250th birthday. “Well, maybe it was just always meant to be now.”

The Movie That Wrote Him

“Do you write the movie or does the movie write you?” Smallbone asks. “There’s never been a movie that’s written me more than Drummer Boy.”

He lists the evidence. “We came up with this rendition of ‘The Little Drummer Boy’ at the beginning of our career. We’re called for KING + COUNTRY, which is a British mantra. We wore these revolutionary-type uniforms for many years. I’m in a band with my brother. This is a movie about brothers on opposite sides of the battlefield. I’m a musician. It’s a musical. You just see all of these breadcrumbs.”

When he got stuck on the lead character, a director asked him who he was. “I’ve got a rescuer complex,” he says. “A bit of a savior complex. And so I just wrote all of it into the film.”

Unsung Hero was literally about his family, so it’s fair to ask why this one feels more like him. His answer is allegory.

“Jesus was the allegory guy,” Smallbone says. “He made up stories for a living, you know? I see myself more in it because it’s all allegorical about our life, and America, and me being an immigrant and in a mixed marriage, and brothers on other sides of the battlefield.”

A Musical for People Who Hate Musicals

“I need to clear up something to the musical haters,” he says. About 30 minutes of the film are musical moments, “very personal expressions of heartache or love or loss.” He calls it “Hamilton meets The Patriot meets Pride and Prejudice.”

His rule for when a character should sing is simple. “The best musicals put language to things that you couldn’t express through dialogue. The worst musicals just sing the whole time. And I’m like, just stop. That’s not life.”

His example is Chris Martin writing “Fix You” after Gwyneth Paltrow’s father died. “You have to express yourself in grief, in pain, and a lot of times it comes through music.”

The same logic runs through the film. One character, an enslaved woman, sings her way through being stuck. “She’s stuck and she’s enslaved and she needs to sing about it to understand it better,” he says.

Two Brothers Behind the Camera

The shoot gave the co-directing brothers plenty of challenges to overcome. The last day of filming was the big argument between Jeremiah and Emmaline on a hillside, in 40 mph winds.

“She’s in this dress, almost getting blown off the hillside,” Smallbone says. “We were like, I don’t know if we’re gonna use any of this.” The wind made the cut. “The tragedy of the bad weather actually created a third layer to the scene.”

The argument matters to the story. Jeremiah, Smallbone says, is “not practicing what he’s preached.” His father taught him “no boy or girl or slave or free, because all in one in Christ are we,” an echo of Galatians 3:28. Jeremiah is “chasing, basically, imperialism and hierarchy and climbing the ladder by who he’s gonna marry.”

Heat was the opposite problem. On a day he puts at 87 degrees, the Irish cast and crew, who spend winter swimming in a rocky ocean, wilted. “You would have thought we were in New Mexico, or Las Vegas on a hot summer,” he says. “A couple of people were hospitalized.”

Drummer Boy had company on the Irish shoot. Smallbone played a villain in a small role in Young Washington, a film about the young George Washington made there, and he’s at peace with the overlap. He points to something Rick Rubin says: “Don’t be upset if that idea that you thought of comes to life through someone else’s vision. It’s not that they stole your idea, it’s that the time had come for the idea.”

Young Washington paid off for him, too. He kept the red British uniform, he says, and “they let me run onto the sets outside of filming, and they let me borrow one of their featured extras” to shoot a sizzle reel that “ended up helping get Drummer Boy funded.” He wandered the island in character and apologized to anyone who gave him a look. “I’d go, ‘Hey, I’m really sorry. I’m Australian. I’m not even from England.’”

Forgiveness is the theme he says he’s proudest of in the film. “What does it mean to be forgiven by God? What does it mean to forgive yourself? What does it mean to forgive others?” Smallbone asks. “You can’t have freedom without forgiveness.”

It was personal for the Smallbones, too. He and Ben had to find their way back to each other before they could make a movie about it. “It was really Drummer Boy when it came back around,” he says, “and we started talking again.”

items.title: Living the Eternal in Flux
items.author: Johan T. Erlandsson-Díaz
items.summary:
Johan T. Erlandsson-Díaz

Some of the hardest crises of belief arise not from hostility to God, but from the wish to remain faithful when the world—or one’s understanding of it—has changed.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Johan T. Erlandsson-Díaz

You will hear of wars and rumors of wars; see that you are not alarmed; for this must take place, but the end is not yet.

—Matt 24:6

To live is to live in flux.

Perhaps that is one reason I became a historian. Much of the work involves spending time among worlds that have disappeared. We read letters written by people who trusted their institutions, inhabited political orders they assumed would last, and understood reality through ideas that later generations would abandon. Every age imagines itself permanent. Many end up as footnotes in one of my unfinished research projects.

It is tempting to think that our own age is unusually unstable. Historians, though, encounter that feeling in almost every period they study. Each generation discovers, often with some surprise, that the world will not stand still. Few songs capture that feeling quite like “Lost Horizons” by the criminally underrated 1990s band Gin Blossoms. It is not so much a protest against change as the sound of someone trying to make a familiar world feel new again. The song’s image of “the gardens and the graves” stays with me: places where life begins and ends, with all of human history unfolding between them.

Heraclitus said that everything flows. History gives us little reason to disagree. Empires fall, revolutions become traditions, and civilizations once thought eternal survive instead in archives, ruins, and the occasional doctoral dissertation. Still, we want something to last, something that will outlive the latest upheaval. Christianity offers an answer that is easy to misunderstand. It does not promise to lift us out of history. It claims that eternity has entered history. The Catholic Modernist Crisis of the early twentieth century makes clear just how difficult that claim can be to grasp.

Much of my work concerns the Modernist Crisis, a painful and complicated episode in Catholic history that came to a head under Pius X. In 1907, Lamentabili Sane Exitu condemned propositions associated with theological modernism; later that year, Pascendi Dominici Gregis called modernism “the synthesis of all heresies.” Alfred Loisy was excommunicated in 1908. George Tyrrell, expelled from the Jesuits and deprived of the sacraments, died the following year and was denied Catholic burial. In 1910, the Oath Against Modernism was imposed on clergy and theologians across much of the Catholic world. These are the familiar milestones. The longer I spend with the sources, however, the more I find myself drawn to the people caught up in the controversy. Their letters do not reveal simply rebels or unbelievers; they show people who wanted to believe and who loved the Church but faced questions they could neither ignore nor easily resolve. Loisy and Tyrrell eventually found themselves outside the Church’s communion. Others, including the English Catholic writer Wilfrid Ward, remained within it while trying to reconcile their faith with what historical study had taught them.

Their difficulties were part of a wider change in how Europeans understood the past. During the nineteenth century, historical criticism, archaeology, philology, and evolutionary theory all made it more difficult to treat institutions, ideas, nations, or even theology as though they had no history. For some Catholics, this new awareness opened up possibilities. For others, it was unsettling, like standing on a floor that had begun to shift beneath them. The old maps were still there, but they no longer seemed to fit the landscape.

I find their experience familiar. The circumstances are different, of course, but we also live with inherited certainties under pressure and with technological and cultural changes that are difficult to make sense of as they happen. Flannery O’Connor writes, “There is no suffering greater than what is caused by the doubts of those who want to believe.” Faith, she suggests, is not a comforting electric blanket but a cross. Some of the hardest crises of belief arise not from hostility to God, but from the wish to remain faithful when the world—or one’s understanding of it—has changed.

Faith is often treated as a refuge from uncertainty, as if religion should offer security and protect us from ambiguity. Scripture tells a less reassuring story. Abraham leaves his homeland without knowing where he is going. Jacob wrestles through the night. Job sits among the ruins and demands answers. The apostles repeatedly misunderstand Jesus, and even after the resurrection, some of them doubt. Faith, in these stories, does not mean that struggle has ended. It means we must try to remain faithful in the midst of the struggle.

There are good reasons why that can be difficult. The twentieth century dealt a heavy blow to easy confidence in progress. The civilization that produced extraordinary scientific advances also produced Verdun, Auschwitz, and the Gulag. The twenty-first century has offered little reason to relax. Our technological powers have grown, but loneliness, fragmentation, and distrust remain. We move quickly and still struggle to know where we are going. Christianity does not deny this instability. Jesus speaks of wars, rumors of wars, persecution, and tribulation; the faith makes no promise that earthly kingdoms or civilizations will last. Its refusal to despair rests on the Incarnation: God has entered the world as it is, not as we wish it were.

Christianity tells not of humanity escaping time to find eternity but of eternity entering time. The Creator enters creation; the eternal Word takes flesh and dwells among us. St. Athanasius is important here: For him, the Incarnation was not simply an intervention in human affairs; it was the healing of humanity from within. His famous claim that God became man so that man might become god can sound like a call to leave the material world behind, but that is not the point. The world is to be transformed, not discarded. Matter matters: God does not save us by pulling us out of creation but by entering it.

This was one of the questions that made the Modernist Crisis so painful. Catholics on different sides of the dispute could come to see history and eternity as competing claims, as though loyalty to one meant surrendering the other. Historical consciousness seemed to threaten permanence; development seemed to threaten continuity; change seemed to threaten truth. John Henry Newman, who died in 1890, had already offered another way to think about the problem. Living things develop: acorns become oak trees, languages change, cultures mature, and institutions take new forms. The question is not whether development happens but whether something recognizably the same can endure through it. For Newman, Christianity did not need to stand outside history to preserve its identity. It could move through history without ceasing to be itself. Wilfrid Ward, Newman’s biographer, returned to this problem repeatedly during the Modernist Crisis.

The Christian task, then, is not to flee history but to look for God’s presence within it. Some sixty years after Pascendi, the Second Vatican Council’s Gaudium et spes called the Church to read the signs of the times while remaining rooted in Christ. The Council recognized both the possibilities and the dangers of the modern world. It refused easy optimism, but it also refused despair, affirming that “only in the mystery of the incarnate Word does the mystery of man take on light.” That is a demanding answer. Neither progress, nostalgia, nor political victory can bear the weight of Christian hope. The answer is Christ.

The sacraments make this claim tangible. History brings change, failure, reform, renewal, conflict, and loss. Yet every Sunday, bread and wine are brought to an altar. They are ordinary things, shaped by the same material world that is always changing. The Church nevertheless proclaims that, here, the eternal becomes present. The Eucharist is not an escape from history but a presence within it, an extension of the Incarnation’s logic. The Word who entered human life continues to meet his people in the midst of it.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

None of this makes life less turbulent. The horizon keeps moving, and history remains unsettled. Joy gives way to grief; laughter is interrupted by bad news; ambitious political projects become questions on future exams. There are late nights spent watching old episodes of Sharpe and hoping, against experience, that Sean Bean might survive this time. And there comes the moment when the slang used by twenty-year-olds sounds less like English than intelligence gathered from a rival civilization.

There are also funerals that come too soon, friendships that fade without anyone quite deciding to let them go, medical results opened with trembling hands, and headlines announcing another war. Loss accumulates over a lifetime. Sometimes the hardest part is realizing that people we love belong increasingly to our memories rather than to our future.

Christianity does not offer a way out of this unfinished world. It makes the stranger claim that God chooses to dwell here, amid confusion and comedy, suffering and waiting. Kingdoms still fall, bodies still fail, and history refuses to stand still. Christ remains present. That does not make every loss easy to understand, but it means that even a lost horizon need not be the end of the road.

Perhaps the horizon still retreats, but it is no longer empty.

items.title: Friday, November 6, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus praises a steward who cheats his master. What do we make of this?
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Philippians 3:17—4:1

Brothers and sisters, join in imitating me, and observe those who live according to the example you have in us. For many live as enemies of the cross of Christ; I have often told you of them, and now I tell you even with tears. Their end is destruction; their god is the belly; and their glory is in their shame; their minds are set on earthly things. But our citizenship is in heaven, and it is from there that we are expecting a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ. He will transform the body of our humiliation that it may be conformed to the body of his glory, by the power that also enables him to make all things subject to himself. Therefore, my brothers and sisters, whom I love and long for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, my beloved.

Psalm
Psalm 122:1-2, 3-4ab, 4cd-5

I was glad when they said to me,
    “Let us go to the house of the Lord!”
Our feet are standing
    within your gates, O Jerusalem.
Jerusalem—built as a city
    that is bound firmly together.
To it the tribes go up,
    the tribes of the Lord,
as was decreed for Israel,
    to give thanks to the name of the Lord.
For there the thrones for judgment were set up,
    the thrones of the house of David.

Gospel Reading
Luke 16:1-8

Then Jesus said to the disciples, “There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was squandering his property. So he summoned him and said to him, ‘What is this that I hear about you? Give me an accounting of your management, because you cannot be my manager any longer.’ Then the manager said to himself, ‘What will I do, now that my master is taking the position away from me? I am not strong enough to dig, and I am ashamed to beg. I have decided what to do so that, when I am dismissed as manager, people may welcome me into their homes.’ So, summoning his master’s debtors one by one, he asked the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’ He answered, ‘A hundred jugs of olive oil.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill, sit down quickly, and make it fifty.’ Then he asked another, ‘And how much do you owe?’ He replied, ‘A hundred containers of wheat.’ He said to him, ‘Take your bill and make it eighty.’ And his master commended the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly; for the children of this age are more shrewd in dealing with their own generation than are the children of light.

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus praises a steward who cheats his master. What do we make of this? It seems so peculiar, especially in Luke’s Gospel, where Jesus has been teaching the radical message of detachment from worldly goods. But here he is giving his approval to a man who clings to wealth in an immoral way. Well, what gives? 

Jesus wants us to see that this steward takes a hard look at his situation and decides to do something about it. Now, the Lord is not telling us to imitate his immorality. But what Jesus admires is his resolve. He knows his own weaknesses, he assesses himself honestly, and then he decides to act.

The Lord told the parable to urge us to carefully examine our spiritual condition. His desire is that we choose to renew our relationship with him. He wants us to take stock of our weaknesses and make a firm resolution to acquire necessary strengths to fix them.

If your prayer life is weak, act to give it new life. If you have not been worshipping fervently at Mass, decide to participate more fully. If you have a broken relationship, repair it. And so on. Decide now, then act.
